intro.beginner: An artificial neural network is built from many simple units connected together, an idea borrowed from real nervous systems. The name comes from biology, but over time the link to biology has become less literal. Here you can try one artificial neuron, see how neurons stack into a deep network, and watch a network being trained.
intro.expert: A network of stacked fully connected layers is commonly called a multilayer perceptron (MLP). Each hidden layer applies an affine transformation followed by a nonlinear activation function, and the operations at every layer are learned jointly from data.

neuron.lede: One artificial neuron takes some numbers in, weighs them, adds them up and gives one number out.

parts.name: Inputs
parts.text: The numbers fed into the neuron. Each one is a feature of the example, such as the area of a house when predicting its price.

parts.name: Weights
parts.text: Each input has its own weight. The weight sets how much that input influences the result.

parts.name: Bias
parts.text: One extra number added to the sum. It sets the value of the weighted sum when every input is zero.

parts.name: Weighted sum
parts.text: The neuron multiplies each input by its weight, adds the results together, then adds the bias.

parts.name: Activation function
parts.text: The activation function decides whether the neuron should be activated, working from the weighted sum plus the bias. It turns that sum into the neuron's output, and most activation functions add nonlinearity.

parts.name: Output
parts.text: The value that comes out of the activation function is called an activation. In a network it is passed on to the next layer.

expert.text: With no activation function, this single unit is linear regression: a single-layer fully connected network with one computed neuron. The inputs are given, not computed, so they are not counted as a layer.

activations.name: Threshold
activations.formula: 0 below the threshold, 1 above it (in this demo the threshold is 0)
activations.text: Gives 0 below a threshold and 1 above it. The first artificial neurons, described by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, were thresholding units like this.

activations.name: Sigmoid
activations.text: Squashes any input into a value between 0 and 1. It is a smooth version of the threshold unit, which suited it to learning with gradients. Its gradient vanishes for large positive and negative inputs, and in hidden layers it has largely been replaced by ReLU.

activations.name: Tanh
activations.text: Shaped like the sigmoid, but it squashes inputs into values between −1 and 1 and is symmetric about the origin.

activations.name: ReLU
activations.text: Keeps positive values and sets negative values to 0. It is the most popular choice because it is simple to implement and performs well on a variety of tasks.

compare.lede: One textbook compares the artificial neuron with a simple picture of a nerve cell. This is how it lines the two up.

rows.text: Information arrives at the dendrites, the cell's input terminals.
rows.link: See dendrites on the real neuron

rows.text: Each arriving signal is weighted by a synaptic weight, which sets whether it excites or inhibits, and how strongly.
rows.link: See the synapse on the real neuron

rows.text: The weighted inputs are added together, in the source's picture inside the nucleus, and may then pass through a nonlinear function.
rows.link: See how a real neuron adds up its inputs

rows.text: The result travels along the axon, the output wire, to the axon terminals, which connect to other neurons through synapses.
rows.link: See the axon on the real neuron

caveat.text: This is a simplified picture, not a model of the brain. The name 'neural network' comes from biology, but the interpretation has become less literal over time. Deep learning now draws at least as much on mathematics, statistics and computer science as on neuroscience. As one textbook comparison puts it, aeroplanes may have been inspired by birds, but the study of birds has not been the main driver of aircraft design for centuries.

network.lede: One neuron can only do so much. Deep networks get their power from stacking many neurons in layers.

points.text: Without an activation function, a neuron is a linear model, and linear models are limited: raising an input can only ever push the output one way, up or down, depending on the sign of its weight.

Adding one or more hidden layers between the input and the output overcomes this limit. The simplest way is to stack fully connected layers, in which every input influences every neuron in the next layer.
The hidden layers need a nonlinear activation function. Without one, the stacked layers collapse into a single linear model and nothing is gained.
Deep learning is called deep because its models learn many layers of transformations, chained one after another.
The layers before the last one act as a learned representation of the data, and the final layer makes the prediction from it. Both are learned together from data instead of being designed by hand.

forward.text: Sending a signal through the network is called forward propagation: values are calculated and stored in order, from the input layer to the output layer.

counting.text: The input layer does no calculation, so it is not counted. A network with one hidden layer and one output layer has two layers.

expert.text: A network built this way is commonly called a multilayer perceptron (MLP). With one hidden layer: H = σ(XW⁽¹⁾ + b⁽¹⁾), O = HW⁽²⁾ + b⁽²⁾.

Universal approximation: results such as Cybenko (1989) suggest that even one hidden layer, given enough neurons and the right weights, can model any function. Learning those weights is the hard part.
Deeper networks can approximate many functions much more compactly than wider ones.

training.lede: Nobody types in the weights. A network is created by training: it typically starts out random and is adjusted, little by little, using examples.

steps.title: Start at random
steps.text: Training starts from a model whose parameters are typically set at random. It cannot do anything useful yet.

steps.title: Take some examples
steps.text: Grab some of the data. In supervised learning each example has features, which are the inputs, and a label, which is the right answer.

steps.title: Measure the error
steps.text: A loss function measures how far the predictions are from the real values. Smaller is better, and a perfect prediction scores 0.

steps.title: Adjust the weights
steps.text: Gradient descent checks, for each parameter, how the loss would change if that parameter were nudged a little, then moves it in the direction that lowers the loss. The learning rate, a small positive number, sets the size of each step.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Take more examples and adjust again, over and over, until the model performs well.

points.text: Parameters are like knobs: turning them changes how the program behaves. Once they are fixed, the program is called a model.

Backpropagation calculates the gradient for every parameter by moving through the network in reverse, from the output layer to the input layer, using the chain rule from calculus. Those gradients are then used to update the parameters.
During training, forward propagation and backpropagation alternate.
A model is checked on test data that was held out from training. A model that does well on its training data but fails on unseen data is overfitting.

expert.text: Squared error for one example: l = ½(ŷ − y)². The training loss is the average over the examples.
Minibatch stochastic gradient descent: sample a random minibatch, compute the gradient of its average loss, multiply by the learning rate η and subtract the result from the parameters.
The learning rate and the minibatch size are set by the user and are not updated in the training loop. Such values are called hyperparameters.

Backpropagation reuses the intermediate values stored during forward propagation, so they must be kept until it finishes. This is one of the reasons training needs significantly more memory than prediction.

demo.title: Train a tiny network
demo.text: This is a real, tiny network running in your browser: 2 inputs, one hidden layer of 4 neurons and 1 output. It has four examples to learn: the answer is 1 when the two inputs differ and 0 when they match. Press Train and watch the loss fall as the weights are adjusted.
demo.note: Illustration only. It uses squared-error loss and gradient descent on all four examples at once.

quiz.q: What does a weight do in an artificial neuron?
options: Sets how much one input influences the result
Stores the training examples
Counts the layers in the network
Decides how long training lasts
quiz.explain: Each input has its own weight, and the weight sets how much that input influences the result.

quiz.q: What does the ReLU activation function do?
options: Squashes every value to between 0 and 1
Keeps positive values and sets negative values to 0
Adds the bias to the sum
Picks the weights at random
quiz.explain: ReLU is max(x, 0): positive values pass through and negative values become 0.

quiz.q: What happens if you stack layers without a nonlinear activation function?
options: The network learns faster
The network needs no training
The layers collapse into a single linear model
The network becomes a model of the brain
quiz.explain: Without a nonlinear activation function the stacked layers are still just one linear model, so nothing is gained.

quiz.q: Why is deep learning called deep?
options: It needs very large computers
Its models learn many layers of transformations
It copies the deepest parts of the brain
Its results are hard to understand
quiz.explain: The models chain many layers of transformations one after another, and that depth gives deep learning its name.

quiz.q: A network's weights at the very start of training are usually…
options: Copied from a real brain
All set to 1
Typed in by an expert
Set at random
quiz.explain: Training typically starts from randomly set parameters and adjusts them step by step using examples.

quiz.q: In which direction does backpropagation move through the network?
options: From the output layer back to the input layer
From the input layer to the output layer
Only within the hidden layers
In a random order
quiz.explain: Backpropagation calculates gradients in reverse order, from the output layer to the input layer, using the chain rule.

quiz.q: What does a loss function measure?
options: How many neurons the network has
How fast the computer is
How far the predictions are from the real values
How many examples are in the dataset
quiz.explain: The loss measures the distance between predicted and real values. Smaller is better, and a perfect prediction scores 0.

glossary.definition: A simple computing unit: it multiplies each input by a weight, adds the results and a bias, and may pass the sum through an activation function.
A number attached to one input of an artificial neuron. It sets how much that input influences the result.
An extra number added to the weighted sum. It sets the value of the sum when every input is zero.
A function applied to a neuron's weighted sum that decides whether the neuron should be activated. Most add nonlinearity.
The activation function max(x, 0): it keeps positive values and sets negative values to 0.
An activation function that squashes any input into a value between 0 and 1.
A layer of neurons between the input and the output of a network.
A network made by stacking fully connected layers, with one or more hidden layers.
Machine learning with models that learn many layers of transformations of the data.
A measure of how far a model's predictions are from the real values. Smaller is better.
A way of training: repeatedly move each parameter a small step in the direction that lowers the loss.
A small positive number that sets the size of each gradient descent step.
Calculating and storing a network's values in order, from the input layer to the output layer.
The method for calculating the gradient of every parameter, working in reverse from the output layer to the input layer with the chain rule.
When a model does well on its training data but fails on data it has not seen.
